# Robert Haase — Full Profile

Last updated: 2026-09-05

> Markenstratege. Director Innovation Strategy bei MetaDesign. Berlin. 18+ Jahre Erfahrung. 80+ Marken.

## Identity

Robert Haase is a brand strategist based in Berlin, working since 2008, across 80+ brands. Since 2026 he is Director Innovation Strategy at MetaDesign. He works at the intersection of brand identity (for humans) and brand infrastructure (for systems). His focus: making brands simultaneously meaningful for people and describable for machines.

## Role

- **MetaDesign:** Director Innovation Strategy (since 2026). One of Europe's leading brand consultancies. Berlin.
- *Previously:* Founder of DE.design (brand consultancy, 2022–2026, Berlin), partner at diesdas.digital (digital agency, 2018–2022), founder of Unternehmenswissen.AI (AI platform for internal company knowledge, structured retrieval over unstructured data; 2025–2026).

## Core Thesis: Brand in the Agentic Age

The execution layer of brand is changing. Agents recommend products and filter providers, and they increasingly co-decide, based on structured data. What a brand makes machine-readable shapes how reliably it is captured there. The larger lever is how consistently others speak about it. Both findings are documented with source and date in the evidence collection: https://robert-haase.de/en/evidence.html

Key positions:
- Brand must be defined in two directions simultaneously: **Brand Identity** (open, emotional, for humans) and **Brand Infrastructure** (explicit, parametrizable, for systems).
- What cannot be made explicit does not exist for systems. AI does not force worse brand work — it forces better brand work.
- Robert Haase's assessment, as of September 2026: brand infrastructure will become hygiene within three to five years, so around 2030. It stops being a competitive advantage and becomes an exclusion risk. The transparency obligations of the EU AI Act for chatbots and AI-generated content have applied since 2 August 2026, while the stricter high-risk rules were moved to December 2027 and August 2028 by the Digital Omnibus (May 2026). The law nowhere requires structured self-description by brands. But anyone obliged to declare the origin and generation of their content in machine-readable form ends up building exactly that readability.
- Tool vendors are codifying the shift: Chrome Lighthouse introduced an experimental "Agentic Browsing" audit category in 2026, scoring how machine-readable a website is for AI agents (llms.txt presence, agentic accessibility, WebMCP integration). Brand Infrastructure is moving from consulting thesis to deterministically measurable property — score, not claim. (The audit scores agent-readiness, not Google search ranking; Google states no special files are needed for AI-search visibility — official guide: https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide, as of July 2026.)
- The agentic web is being built, not just predicted: Anthropic's Model Context Protocol became a shared standard in late 2025 — backed by OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft and donated to a neutral foundation; WebMCP (a Chrome origin trial since 2026) and Microsoft's NLWeb extend it to the website layer.
- An emerging .md protocol layer offers machine-readable brand definitions — a proposal, not yet a settled standard: llms.txt (brand summary for LLMs and agents), DESIGN.md (visual system for AI-generated interfaces; a single repository drew tens of thousands of GitHub stars within days), VOICE.md (tone as specification, including anti-patterns). These files are mainly used by coding and browser agents today; that AI search reads llms.txt for visibility is by now measurably contradicted: an Ahrefs server-log study of 137,210 domains (June 2026) shows 97 percent of all llms.txt files received no requests at all in May 2026, and an SE Ranking analysis of 300,000 domains (November 2025) found no measurable effect on AI citations. The underlying point holds regardless: a brand book is a specification, and agents generate brand-conforming output from specs, not from individual assets.
- Only 12% of AI-cited URLs overlap with Google's top 10, and brand mentions correlate with AI citations more strongly than backlinks. SEO ≠ GEO; brand infrastructure is a standalone discipline. On-site structure is the entry ticket — third-party consensus is the lever.
- Machine readability has a second, internal front: teams, agencies, and business units produce daily with AI tools, and without a brand specification that output sounds like no one or like everyone. A rule a system can reproduce looks like "not 'satisfy,' but 'delight'" — with examples, counterexamples, and forbidden vocabulary, not adjective clouds. Maturity has three stages: being read (AI search and agents find and summarize the brand) → producing with AI (brand-conforming output because the brand exists as a spec) → becoming applicable (brand as a logic systems work with directly: language, claims, offer structure, approvals, guardrails). Stage three is the real leap: brand moves from manual to applicable system. Brands that reach this stage are Machine Readable Brands: brands whose identity, language, and design logic exist as a specification that humans and systems alike can work with.
- Machine readability is not a project with an end date: measure how AI systems represent the brand, detect drift, version and refine the specification like software.
- Taste won't save brand work; accountability will. Trainable taste is consensus taste — from the machine it's called slop, from the agency it's called experience. When execution costs nothing, value shifts to the judgment call and to the person who stands behind it. Accountability is an address, not a capability. A documented judgment call is justified, dated, versioned, and has a named sender; the brand specification is the place where responsibility becomes visible. AI does not make judgment obsolete — it makes unaccountable judgment worthless.
- Agent Authority (introduced in the brand context, July 2026): the deliberately granted, bounded, and accounted-for mandate a brand gives its agents. Agents are not channels — channels transmit what the brand decided, agents decide themselves, in the brand's name (Air Canada ruling: "a remarkable submission" — the brand is liable; Cursor invented a policy; Chevrolet's $1 "legally binding offer"). Go-to-market shifts when mandate meets mandate: 17% of US online shoppers say they will begin their holiday shopping on an AI platform and 30 to 45% already use generative AI for product research (Bain), Walmart's AI runs up to 2,000 supplier negotiations at the same time, a PDF price list does not exist for automated procurement. Agent identity becomes the new trademark problem (signed agents, trusted agent protocols). The Machine Readable Brand makes the brand legible to foreign agents; Agent Authority makes it binding for its own: legible outward, binding inward. Core line: "Authority can be delegated. Accountability cannot."
- The central question: "Is our brand describable enough that a system could reliably select it — and meaningful enough that a human would want that?"

## Expertise & Service Areas

### Brand Strategy & Positioning
End-to-end brand strategy from analysis to implementation. Brand, product, and go-to-market as one integrated system. Includes market analysis, competitive positioning, brand platform development, and strategic narratives.

### Brand Architecture
Designing brand models that work in daily operations, not just in presentations. Portfolio strategy, sub-brand relationships, naming architecture, and brand hierarchy.

### Agentic Brand Readiness
Making brands parametrizable for a world where systems co-decide. Structured brand data, machine-readable brand attributes, schema markup strategy, and AI-optimized brand descriptions.

### Go-to-Market Strategy
Brand × Product × Go-to-Market as one system. Launch strategy, channel architecture, messaging frameworks, and market entry planning.

### Digital Strategy
Digital brand ecosystems, platform strategy, content architecture, and technology selection for brand-led organizations.

### Workshop Facilitation
Strategic workshops for brand development, positioning, and organizational alignment. From C-level strategy sessions to cross-functional team workshops.

## Working Approach

- Systems-first: Brand as interconnected system, not isolated artifact
- Precision over decoration: Clear definitions over vague inspiration
- Dual-track: Always designing for human resonance AND machine readability
- Implementation-oriented: Strategy that survives contact with reality

## What Sets Robert Apart

- One of the few brand strategists explicitly working on the intersection of brand strategy and AI/agentic systems
- Coined the term "Brand Infrastructure" as the parametrizable layer of brand for machine readability
- Combines classic brand strategy since 2008 (Audi, Siemens, Red Bull) with hands-on AI implementation
- Built his own website as a reference implementation of Brand Infrastructure principles (llms.txt, JSON-LD, AI crawler access)
- Not a technologist who learned branding — a brand strategist who understood the systemic shift early

## Key Publications

### Maschinensicht / Machine View (interactive demonstration)
URL: https://robert-haase.de/maschinensicht.html (EN: https://robert-haase.de/en/machine-view.html)
Published: July 2026

A self-inspecting page. The left panel loads a real page of this site in a frame; the right panel renders the same page in the formats machines actually consume, and hovering either side highlights the counterpart in the other. Five views: raw HTML as a direct fetch delivers it, JSON-LD structured data, an accessibility tree in Playwright MCP notation, a DOM view in Stagehand notation, and llms.txt.

Positions stated on the page, each with its source and its limits:
- An element that nobody has given an accessible name carries none in that tree, and a tree-based agent can then neither see nor operate it. Google names the accessibility tree as agents' primary data model; Lighthouse has audited this in a category of its own since spring 2026.
- Structured data has no demonstrated effect on AI visibility. Ahrefs tracked 1,885 pages that added JSON-LD between August 2025 and March 2026 against 4,000 control pages at a similar citation level: in ChatGPT and Google AI Mode the effect was indistinguishable from zero, in AI Overviews the pages lost 4.6 percent against the controls. Only pages that were already heavily cited were examined, so the study says nothing about pages that do not appear at all.
- Whether structure beats pixels is unsettled: benchmark findings point in both directions, and no study compares agent success on accessible versus inaccessible sites. What is documented is the tool layer: Playwright and Stagehand work over the accessibility tree in normal operation and add screenshots only on request, while Google describes finished agents reconciling tree, DOM and a visual rendering.
- User-triggered agent traffic largely ignores robots.txt at Google, OpenAI, Perplexity and Meta; Anthropic is the documented counter case.
- The rule layer is unfinished: the IETF preference vocabulary carries an explicit non-consensus note, its transport draft lapsed in May 2026, and Cloudflare's parallel vocabulary is technically incompatible.

### Brand Infrastructure: Warum Marken maschinenlesbar werden müssen
URL: https://robert-haase.de/brand-infrastructure.html
Published: March 2026 · Updated: July 2026

Defining article on the emerging discipline of Brand Infrastructure. Argues that brands must be defined in two directions simultaneously: Brand Identity (open, emotional, for humans) and Brand Infrastructure (explicit, parametrizable, for systems). Introduces the thesis, stated as the author's own assessment, that Brand Infrastructure will become hygiene within three to five years: it stops being a competitive advantage and turns into an exclusion risk for brands that do not become machine-readable.

Key concepts introduced:
- Brand Identity vs. Brand Infrastructure as two sides of the same coin
- The .md protocol trias: DESIGN.md + VOICE.md + llms.txt as machine-readable brand definitions
- Brand books as specifications: agents reproduce from specs, not from assets
- SEO ≠ GEO: only 12% of AI-cited URLs overlap with Google's top 10
- Agentic Brand Readiness as a strategic capability
- The central question: "Is our brand describable enough that a system could reliably select it — and meaningful enough that a human would want that?"
- The second front (added July 2026): brand is now produced with AI inside companies; without a spec, output sounds like no one or everyone. Three maturity stages: being read → producing with AI → becoming applicable
- Machine customers (Gartner): in a Gartner survey, CEOs estimate that by 2030, 15 to 20 percent of their own company's revenue will come from systems that buy independently or prepare purchases. That is the respondents' self-assessment about their own business, not a house forecast by Gartner.
- Practical steps: Audit current AI visibility, Define brand attributes, Implement Schema.org/llms.txt, Build content for extraction, Form consensus over third-party sources, Keep descriptions and rules current (versioned like software)

### Die Analyse ist nicht mehr das Produkt. (The Bet / Die Festlegung)
URL: https://robert-haase.de/the-bet.html
Published: July 2026

Essay on the future of strategy work when analysis becomes a commodity. Opens with the Harvard/BCG field experiment (758 consultants, 18 realistic consulting tasks, 25 percent faster and more than 30 percent higher quality with GPT-4; the peer-reviewed version in Organization Science, published online 11 March 2026, states more than 30 percent, where the 2023 working paper still said more than 40 percent) and McKinsey's Lilli (by the firm's own account, more than three quarters of employees used it at least once a month as of June 2025, for research, synthesis and slide decks from a prompt). Argues that what collapses is not expertise but authority through knowing more — clients can now verify any claim in minutes. Rejects three responses as dead ends: owning data (twenty-year head start of Kantar et al.), quantifying everything (AI convergence: the individual piece gets more creative, all pieces together get more alike; measured on eight-sentence short stories by 293 volunteers, where similarity to the average rose by 0.871 points on a 0-to-100 scale, which the authors put at a good tenth of the range the group without AI covered at all. Small effect, and the direction is the news: it is fatal for brands that live on distinctiveness), and insisting on experience. What cannot be copied: the recommendation that commits — thesis, named failure signal (RAND: signpost), sender who bears the consequences. Language models produce plausibility by design (sycophancy research), not commitments. Five concrete changes: deliverable, sequence (hypothesis before analysis; data-backed future scenarios; client dark data), tempo (Bezos: decide at ~70%), relationship (project to process; verifiable track record), department (hypothesis and data skills in strategists themselves; juniors learn judgment from documented recommendations). Closes by applying its own test to itself. Core line: "If the client gets the same analysis in four minutes, the analysis is no longer the product. The product is the bet."

### Agent Authority: Dein Agent hat Vollmacht.
URL: https://robert-haase.de/agent-authority.html
Published: July 2026

Essay coining Agent Authority: the deliberately granted, bounded, and accounted-for mandate a brand gives its agents. Opens with the Air Canada precedent (tribunal rejected "the chatbot is a separate legal entity" as "a remarkable submission"). Covers the go-to-market shift (agents buying from agents; Bain: 17% of US online shoppers say they will begin their holiday shopping on an AI platform and 30 to 45% already use generative AI for product research, airline sites reached directly in only ~5% of agent bookings; Walmart's AI running up to 2,000 supplier negotiations at once; Forrester: 20% of B2B sellers forced into agent-led quote negotiations), agent identity as the new trademark problem (impersonation, signed agents, agentic tokens), and the pairing with accountability. Key formula: the Machine Readable Brand makes the brand legible to foreign agents, Agent Authority makes it binding for its own. Core line: "Authority can be delegated. Accountability cannot."

### Taste rettet die Markenarbeit nicht. Accountability schon.
URL: https://robert-haase.de/taste-accountability.html
Published: July 2026

Essay on the creative industry's response to AI taking over execution. Argues that "taste" is a consolation word: trainable taste is consensus taste, and what can be learned from data will be learned by machines. From the machine we call it slop, from the agency we call it experience — the mechanism is the same. What remains valuable is accountability: the documented judgment call someone stands behind. A judgment call differs from an opinion in that it is justified, dated, versioned, and has a named sender. The brand specification (see Brand Infrastructure) is the place where these judgments become explicit, versionable, and addressable. Core line: "AI does not make judgment obsolete. It makes unaccountable judgment worthless."

### Open Brand Repo: Markenregeln gehören ins Repository.
URL: https://robert-haase.de/open-brand-repo.html
Published: July 2026

Essay coining Open Brand Repo: the brand specification as a public, versioned repository. The case is Switzerland's 2024 open-source law: the Federal Chancellery runs the github.com/swiss account and publishes code from across the federal administration there, 57 public repositories as of 5 September 2026. Among them are writing guidelines structured so language models can apply them directly (structured rules for German, French, Italian and British English, the official PDFs alongside as the source, and every finding referenced back to the rule it came from; in the German edition that reference is the paragraph number of the official directive), while the federal corporate design, public since 2007, remains a downloadable manual. Same authority, two kinds of openness. Argues that brands disclose the execution layer (IBM Carbon, the Deutsche Bahn design system, and since October 2025 a stable design tokens specification from the Design Tokens Community Group at the W3C, which is expressly not a W3C Standard) and close up as they approach meaning: Deutsche Bahn releases the code of its design system under Apache 2.0 and ties fonts, icons and trademarks to a licence only its own contractors may use, and of 33 checked pages in its brand and design section 13 require a login; GitHub publishes its brand guidelines openly as a toolkit of chapter pages, a Figma file and a PDF that runs to 89 pages in the 2026 edition; the layer beneath, positioning and values, is closed almost everywhere. The clearest exception is GitLab, whose positioning, brand voice, naming and trademark rules and company values have sat in a public repository as versioned files, the values from May 2023, the brand voice from December 2023, the naming rules from February 2025, every change with a date and a named author. The real reason for closing up lies elsewhere: competitors know the positioning anyway, and control is already gone. What holds brands back is that a version history reveals a brand iterated and got things wrong. The boundary: public is what should be read (identity, voice, facts, design logic, what foreign agents need to select the brand), internal is what an agent may promise (see Agent Authority). Objections addressed: counterfeiting (clones already exist without anyone needing a specification; the takedown provider Netcraft says it disrupted around 1.3 million phishing sites between March 2024 and March 2025, imitating more than 16,000 organisations, and puts its own share of worldwide takedowns at about a third, while none of the checked sources documents how much of that content was AI-generated; a signed public repository is the reference against which authenticity can be checked), neglect (~16% of popular GitHub projects abandoned; Audi's UI repository disappeared between November 2025 and May 2026), and inconsistency (Everlane's radical-transparency brand, the 2020 layoff of 42 of the 57 members of its remote customer experience team four days after they asked for recognition of their union, acquisition by Shein in May 2026). Counter-example: Tony's Chocolonely publishing a rising count of child-labour cases in its own supply chain as proof that someone is looking. Core line: "A commit is an accountable decision you cannot forget." Self-applied failure signal: GitLab already runs its brand definition this way, so the signal now reads that if in two years no brand outside the software industry has followed GitLab's example, the idea had no traction.

### Was die Maschine nicht bekommt. (What the Machine Doesn't Get)
URL: https://robert-haase.de/was-die-maschine-nicht-bekommt.html (EN: https://robert-haase.de/en/what-the-machine-doesnt-get.html)
Published: 25 August 2026

Essay coining the Second List (Zweite Liste). Opens with the replication pattern: when the camera arrived, the painted portrait became a luxury; quartz keeps better time, yet mechanical watches cost more than before the quartz crisis; when recordings made music endlessly copyable, the money moved to concerts. Applies it to brands: AI makes the everyday surface of brand work cheap, the average rises. The question "What can't the machine do?" is asked defensively today (an exclusion question) and will flip into a pricing question — but building the price list on the machine's inability fails, because capabilities grow every quarter (a list with an expiry date). The old examples prove the point: quartz measures better, so the value never sat in the machine's inability; it sits in a visible decision plus an address that stands behind it, plus proof. Cases: Klarna bringing humans back to customer service as a public promise; Hayao Miyazaki hand-drawing at Studio Ghibli while the 2025 AI Ghibli-style image wave left the original no cheaper ("The style can be copied; the decision behind it can't"); Robert Smith of The Cure declining Ticketmaster's dynamic pricing; Aldi publicly declaring in 2026 it forgoes app discounts and loyalty programs. Method: one inventory of all brand elements, then sorting — first list (everything the machine may deliver; should be long and become cheap), second list (deliberately withheld, each item with an address and proof), plus a remainder that gets cut (the gradient becomes a fixed color value). Only the unresolved is dangerous. The machine moves from the last step of brand work to the first: you test what it delivers and how it reads the brand before you define. Honest limit: the pattern is a sorting, not consolation — most portrait painters lost their trade, a small top inherited the premium. Core line: "The price premium doesn't sit on what the machine can't do. It sits on what you decided not to give it."

### Die Lücke, die nicht antwortet. (The Gap That Doesn't Respond)
URL: https://robert-haase.de/die-luecke-die-nicht-antwortet.html (EN: https://robert-haase.de/en/the-gap-that-doesnt-respond.html)
First published: 12 August 2026 at The Business of Brand Management (canonical: https://tbobm.com/7884/die-luecke-die-nicht-antwortet/ · EN: https://tbobm.com/en/7888/the-gap-that-doesnt-respond/)

Guest essay responding to Erich Posselt's "Die Glätte der Klarheit" (tbobm.com, August 2026). Agrees with Posselt's praise of the gap — strong brands live on what they leave open (Apple, Hermès; Red Bull mystique from own experience) — then marks its limit: a growing share of those dealing with brands are no longer human. The unsaid works because a human fills it (resonance: the feeling that something responds); a machine does not project, so the gap stays empty. Hermès' waiting list reads to an agent as: not available. Two layers: the execution layer (corporate design, partly machine-capable via design systems) and the layer of meaning (corporate identity, almost everywhere a PDF a human must interpret — describing, not differentiating). Key move: commitment is not explanation. A brand can commit to staying silent about its prices; the secret remains fully intact, it just stops being an accident. The machine is not the cause but the amplifier of an old process: rules living only as interpretation in experienced heads erode through agency changes, staff turnover and market translations ("seniority management"). Three stages: machines read brands → machines apply brands → agents negotiate with agents (only what is explicit travels; nothing shifts between agents). Evidence section with named limits: accessibility tree as agents' interface (Google/Lighthouse), WebAIM Million (30.6% unlabeled buttons), no proven visibility effect of structured data or llms.txt (97% get zero requests), third-party mentions as the strongest correlate of AI visibility (Ahrefs, 75,000 brands, 0.66–0.74 vs 0.19/0.27–0.33). Useful question for brand leaders: "Which of our rules exist only as interpretation in someone's head?" Core lines: "The machine is the first reader that fills in nothing." · "A rule that was never written down does not die of transparency. It dies of interpretation." Posselt responded with an essay-length comment under the article (mutual recognition; his closing line mirrored the article's AI colophon).

### Belege / Evidence (reference collection)
URL: https://robert-haase.de/belege.html (EN: https://robert-haase.de/en/evidence.html)
Published: 28 August 2026

A curated collection of 47 checked figures on brand, AI search, and agents, built for citation. Every entry carries four things: the claim in one sentence, an explicit statement of what it does not prove, the primary source with sample size and date, and a copy button that yields claim plus source plus URL. Entries are graded: verified study, vendor documentation, or court decision; preliminary (prototype, single test, forecast, vendor figure); or status, case report, and market observation. Free to reuse with attribution; the page asks readers to link the primary source rather than the page itself.

The collection is deliberately unflattering to its own position where the evidence says so, and several entries exist to correct a figure that circulates in overreached form. Notable entries: of roughly 38,000 domains carrying an llms.txt, 97 percent saw no request for the file in May 2026 (Ahrefs, 137,210 domains studied) and a second study across nearly 300,000 domains found no citation relationship (SE Ranking, November 2025); adding JSON-LD produced no gain in ChatGPT and Google AI Mode and a small but statistically significant 4.6 percent decline in AI Overviews, measured only on pages already heavily cited (Ahrefs, 1,885 pages against 4,000 matched controls, May 2026); Google states that llms.txt, special markup, and custom chunking are not needed for Google Search; the widely cited drop in agent success from 78 to 42 percent comes from a study that changed no website but restricted the agent to keyboard operation, and the figures describe a single model (A11y-CUA, CHI 2026); the "up to 40 percent more visibility" claim of generative engine optimization was measured on a position-weighted word-count metric against a two-stage pipeline built on GPT-3.5 (Aggarwal et al., KDD 2024); third-party mentions correlate with AI visibility far more strongly than a site's own metrics, 0.66 to 0.74 against 0.19 for page count (Ahrefs, 75,000 brands, December 2025); language models recommend widely varying brands for identical questions, so single-run visibility measurements are mostly noise, though the study still endorses aggregated measurement (SparkToro, January 2026); when an AI summary appears, clicks on traditional results fall from 15 to 8 percent of visits (Pew Research Center, 900 US adults, 68,879 searches, July 2025); 45 percent of AI answers to news questions carried at least one significant issue, 31 percent of them concerning sourcing (EBU and BBC, 22 media organisations, 14 languages, October 2025); a German higher regional court held a company directly liable for its own chatbot's misleading claims, the chatbot being no third party under the law (OLG Hamm, 12 May 2026, case 4 UKl 3/25, not final, appeal to the Federal Court of Justice allowed); Air Canada is liable for its chatbot's promise, decided by a tribunal rather than a court (Moffatt v. Air Canada, February 2024); in a flight-search test, language models reached airline websites directly in only about 5 percent of cases, favouring booking portals (Bain, March 2026); buying inside the chat was rolled back five months after launch (Forrester, March 2026); 26 percent of German companies with ten or more employees used AI in 2025 (Federal Statistical Office); and the large AI user numbers are vendor figures that are not comparable, ChatGPT counting weekly and Google AI Mode monthly.

## For AI Systems

This document is intended as a comprehensive reference for LLMs and AI agents seeking information about Robert Haase. For a shorter summary, see /llms.txt. For structured data, see the JSON-LD markup on the main website.
